articles.title: Smart adaptive headlights are finally coming to the US
articles.summary: The NHTSA has ruled on amending FMVSS 108 to allow Adaptive Driving Beam technology in the US. The move stems from a requirement in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.
articles.body: The National Highway and Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) announced a final ruling this week that permits automakers to finally add Adaptive Driving Beams (ADB) for vehicles on US roads. Adaptive headlights, available on many vehicles in Europe, Canada, and Japan, have been prohibited in the US due to rigid and outdated federal regulations. Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (standard no. 108) specified requirements for lamps and reflectors dating back to 1967, which standardized binary hi / low beams, which as a result stifled newer headlight technology. But now, after the passage of President Joe Biden’s $1 trillion infrastructure bill late last year, NHTSA was directed to amend FMVSS no. 108. The agency was given two years to take action but was able to make the change a year and a half ahead of schedule. NHTSA claims that the final rule will improve safety for pedestrians and bicyclists by making them more visible at night and will help prevent crashes by better illuminating animals and objects in and along the road. “NHTSA prioritizes the safety of everyone on our nation’s roads, whether they are inside or outside a vehicle. New technologies can help advance that mission,” said Steven Cliff, NHTSA’s Deputy Administrator, in a statement. Adaptive Driving Beams are a headlight technology with automated beamforming, controlled by a computer that aims lights in different directions. It can brighten your path directly ahead and dim the lights that shine outward that could blind oncoming drivers. In its final ruling, NHTSA sought to “ensure that ADB systems do not increase glare to other motorists beyond current lower beams,” which was a concern when the agency previously assessed the technology in 2015. [Image: Audi’s Digital Matrix LED is an ADB system that can form a light “carpet” on the road ahead using almost one million micro mirrors. Since that last assessment, AAA conducted comparative research of US and European headlamps in 2019, concluding that European vehicles equipped with ADB “less frequently” produced glare to oncoming drivers when cresting hills versus US vehicles without the feature. But automakers have had to hold back the advanced lighting technology in the US and instead include features like cornering or curving headlights, in which the beam turned in the direction of travel, as well as automatic high beams. Some drivers have found automatic high beams frustrating, though, because of how often they can misread oncoming traffic and start strobing. Many modern American vehicles are equipped with automatic hi-beams, including Lincoln MKZs, Tesla Model 3s, and even Chrysler Pacifica minivans, which can behave erratically when trying to interpret oncoming headlights as compared to other lights and reflections. This is where ADB really shines: it can keep the central beam, providing excellent visibility ahead while dimming the extremities of the beam “cone” to keep oncoming traffic from getting blinded. There are also even more advanced ADB systems like Audi’s Digital Matrix headlights in the latest E-tron models, which can create a “carpet” of brighter light ahead, and even widen the beam to another lane in preparation for a lane change. Expect to see ADB in new model year vehicles in the US as early as later this year. Ideally, it will come standard to more vehicles instead of being locked behind a paywall like BMW has done for its auto high beam feature.

articles.title: Poll: Democrats hold major advantage on health care costs
articles.summary: Health care costs remain a top affordability concern for voters, who trust Democrats over Republicans on the issue by a nearly two-to-one margin, according to a new poll from health research group KFF. Six in 10 voters said they are worried about being able to afford their health care, including the cost of health insurance…
articles.body:
Health care costs remain a top affordability concern for voters, who trust Democrats over Republicans on the issue by a nearly two-to-one margin, according to a new poll from health research group KFF.

Six in 10 voters said they are worried about being able to afford their health care, including the cost of health insurance and out-of-pocket prices for things like office visits and prescription drugs. About half of voters said it is “extremely important” for candidates in the midterm elections to talk about the cost of health care, the survey found.

Health costs were tied with gas prices for the most important affordability issue, a finding that’s been consistent across polls for much of the year.

A quarter of voters said they are “very worried” about being able to afford the cost of health care and gas and transportation, and an additional third said they are “somewhat worried” about health care and gas costs.

“Of all the cost-of-living worries hitting voters now, a big health care bill is the least predictable, and that’s a big reason why health care costs are right up there with gas prices and the costs of food and housing on voters’ minds,” KFF President and CEO Drew Altman said in a statement.

The Democratic advantage on health costs has grown over the past six months. In April, Democrats held an eleven-percentage point advantage over Republicans, at 37 percent and 26 percent, respectively. In September, it was a 20-point difference, 42 percent to 22 percent.

Among independent voters, the poll of 1,328 U.S. adults showed Democrats hold at least a two-to-one trust advantage over Republicans on health care costs; though large shares of independents said they didn’t trust either party on most midterm election issues.

The One Big Beautiful Bill, Republicans’ signature legislation, slashed spending on Medicaid and other entitlement programs to fund tax cuts and is proving to be a fertile ground for Democratic attacks. In key battleground states, Democrats are hammering their opponents for voting to cut Medicaid and for allowing enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies to expire, driving up premium costs.

“I think it really is a reflection that this is an affordability election, and Democrats are campaigning on that, whereas Republicans seem to be talking more about fraud, waste, and abuse,” said Shannon Schumacher, a senior survey analyst for the Public Opinion and Survey Research program at KFF and lead author of the poll.

Republicans have historically polled better on economic issues, while voters typically say they trust Democrats more on health issues. But Schumacher noted health costs are a bridge issue, so it’s significant that Democrats have an advantage.

“Republican voters want to hear more about fraud in government programs … it’s an issue that fits well with the base,” Schumacher said. “But when we look at voters as a larger group to include Democrats and Independents as well, we see that cost of living and healthcare costs … are weighing very heavily on voters this year, and frustration with the system at large is really widespread.”

For instance, when asked what they want to hear from a candidate about health costs, the most common responses across parties were related to a desire to hear about candidates’ plans for how they will lower health care costs for people.

“Lowering [health care costs] for people who can’t afford to pay expensive costs for health care,” said a 40-year-old Republican from Arkansas.

There is bipartisan support among the public for major changes to the country’s health care system, though a partisan divide about how to do it.

Some progressive Democrats have been campaigning on Medicare for All , or some form of universal health care, as the solution to high health costs.

According to the poll, public support for Medicare-for All is 66 percent, the highest since 2016. Support drops when people hear criticisms commonly made by opponents about the potential for higher taxes, longer wait times, or threats to the current Medicare program.

On the other hand, support increases when people hear claims made by proponents such as guaranteeing health insurance as a right for all Americans, or eliminating health insurance premiums and reducing out-of-pocket care healthcare costs.

The survey was conducted September 16 through September 21. The margin of sampling error is plus or minus 3 percentage points.

articles.title: Rising Water Bills Have Added to the Squeeze on American Households
articles.summary: Water costs increased by 62% over the past decade, outpacing overall inflation and grocery prices, according to new research by Food & Water Watch.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Water is becoming less affordable for American families as aging infrastructure, pollution rules and climate change push household bills higher — with the artificial intelligence boom adding new pressure on some local water systems.

US household drinking-water bills rose about 62% over the past decade, according to a report released Tuesday by Food & Water Watch, an environmental advocacy group. That increase compares with a roughly 39% jump in overall consumer prices and a 30% rise in grocery prices over roughly the same period, the report says. Water costs also outpaced growth in household income.

Food & Water Watch determined that water bills were unaffordable for low-income households in nearly all the systems it analyzed. "An unaffordable bill is often an unpaid bill," said Mary Grant, water policy director at Food & Water Watch. Customers who fall behind can face shutoffs or, in some jurisdictions, liens on their homes, she said.

The group also found that charges varied enormously. Two large West Virginia systems — both owned by the same private company — billed customers for an average of $1,383 a year. But for customers of three large water systems in Idaho, the annual average was $286, about one-fifth as much.

Food & Water Watch collected rate information from 500 of the nation's largest community water systems, serving 155 million people in total. The group then compared the results to those of its last water study, conducted a decade ago. It was able to do an apples-to-apples comparison between 452 systems in 2015 and 2025, after accounting for consolidations and other changes in the sector.

Differences in water sources, infrastructure age and system size can contribute to the variation in cost. So can ownership. For-profit systems charged more than publicly owned utilities, the report authors found. Private systems – which accounted for about 11% of the systems studied – were disproportionately represented among the most expensive.

But private and public systems alike had common troubles: "It's aging infrastructure. It's federal disinvestment," Grant said. Dealing with chemical contamination and adapting to drought, storms and wildfires is expensive, she added.

images.caption: A glass is filled with water in Long Island, New York. · Bloomberg · Photographer: Steve Pfost/Newsday/ Getty Images

articles.title: Trump’s Golden Dome faces headwinds with funding uncertain
articles.summary: The Golden Dome, President Trump’s lofty plan for a national ballistic missile defense shield, is facing heavy headwinds with project funding still uncertain. The missile defense program, estimated to cost some $1.2 trillion over 20 years of development and operation, needs a significant influx of funding to get it off the ground this fiscal year. …
articles.body:
The Golden Dome, President Trump’s lofty plan for a national ballistic missile defense shield, is facing heavy headwinds with project funding still uncertain.

The missile defense program, estimated to cost some $1.2 trillion over 20 years of development and operation, needs a significant influx of funding to get it off the ground this fiscal year.

But the Pentagon made a risky move in its budget strategy, requesting a $1.15 trillion base budget and a $350 billion reconciliation package to be passed on a party-line vote. The bulk of the Golden Dome funding in fiscal year 2027 is in the reconciliation tranche, raising doubts about whether a lame-duck Congress will be able to inject the program with the dollars it needs to proceed.

Thomas Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said that, as of Thursday — the start of the fiscal year — “the program has no money.”

“This stands or falls with FY-27 appropriations, and I said that’s the single most urgent thing for Golden Dome,” he told The Hill. “It is life and death from that standpoint. Without money there’s no program, it’s just PowerPoint slides.”

The Senate Armed Services subcommittee raised this issue numerous times during a Sept. 29 hearing, at which Karako testified.

“Should it have been necessary to go to a reconciliation to get this started? I would say no. This should have been on a bipartisan basis,” Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said at the hearing. “I won’t lay fault for why that isn’t happening, I’m just simply saying we need to get back to a bipartisan approach to this as soon as possible.”

The subpanel’s ranking member, Sen. Angus King (I-Maine), said the effort is one of the “most expensive and largest projects ever undertaken by the United States government,” making it “very bothersome” that the Trump administration didn’t resource it via the traditional appropriations process.

Trump announced in January 2025 that the Pentagon would build an expansive homeland missile shield intended to protect the skies over the continental U.S. using a network of space-based missiles launched from satellites to intercept missiles launched from the ground.

The Trump administration has insisted the expensive, untested technology is necessary to protect against ballistic, hypersonic, advanced cruise missiles, as well as other next-generation aerial attacks.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) in May estimated that Golden Dome will cost about $1.2 trillion to develop, deploy and operate over the next 20 years. Broken down, that includes $740 billion for a space-based missile warning and tracking system, $270 billion for multiple layers of ground-based defenses and $180 billion for other activities — including deploying a sensor system and conducting research and development.

Space Force Gen. Michael Guetlein, who is overseeing the program, estimated in March that the missile defense system will cost just $185 billion .

To fund the effort, Trump-aligned Republicans included $24.4 billion for the project in their “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” which the president signed in July 2025.

Then, in March, Congress gave the Pentagon $22.5 billion to begin building Golden Dome through a reconciliation bill, but Guetlein this summer said 90 percent of that money was obligated in less than six months.

This year , the Pentagon requested $17 billion for Golden Dome as part of the proposed $350 billion reconciliation package, with only $400 million for the program in the base budget. The strategy leaves Golden Dome in a vulnerable position, as Congress appears to have little desire to pass another spending bill through reconciliation.

Adding to the program’s challenges is the federal government operation under a continuing resolution, a stopgap funding measure that began on Oct. 1 and holds spending at prior year levels — as part of a bipartisan deal to prevent a government shutdown.

Guetlein in August had warned a continuing resolution “doesn’t help me under Golden Dome because I don’t have a topline to fall back to to get that percentage of the continuing resolution.”

If Congress can’t find a route to fund the program, “there is no Golden Dome because there is no funding,” he added.

Lawmakers this week also seem unsure exactly what the system will provide beyond what the U.S. military already gives to homeland defenses — a glaring question at the center of the Senate hearing last week.

In his opening testimony, Karako said Golden Dome “suffers from a serious lack of strategic messaging and explanation of what it is and what it’s trying to do.”

Without that messaging, the references to the program “conjure up fanciful ideas and memes. Critics and cheerleaders project onto it their fears or fantasies, and political polarization doesn’t help,” he said.

King later questioned whether Trump’s executive order, which says Golden Dome will deter and defend U.S. citizens and critical infrastructure, creates an expectation of nationwide shield that the senator said is “just not in the cards.”

“One of the questions that has to be discussed is whose being projected? And what is the Golden Dome actually going to do?” King asked. “Who decides who is protected and who isn’t?”

Karako suggested that Golden Dome as proposed would give protections to certain major cities and critical infrastructure rather than provide a shield over the entire country.

He later told The Hill the U.S. military has “almost nothing” for aerial threats beyond a ballistic missile or bomber aircraft, including drones and cruise missiles.

“It’s not that it can’t be seen; it can be,” he said of the threats. “We just have to be looking for it.”

“We have to have different kinds of sensors, and we have to have them looking in the right place, and we have to be telling them to beep and squawk when the more fulsome spectrum of threats is seen,” he continued, adding that Golden Dome could fill that void.

articles.title: Hegseth’s get-out-the-vote effort draws praise and skepticism
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is ramping up his get-out-the-vote campaign, urging U.S. troops to register to vote in the 2026 midterm elections but not telling them which way to vote. He also issued a stand-down order, allowing service members to get one day off this month to cast a ballot. Critics view Hegseth’s increased emphasis…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is ramping up his get-out-the-vote campaign, urging U.S. troops to register to vote in the 2026 midterm elections but not telling them which way to vote.

He also issued a stand-down order , allowing service members to get one day off this month to cast a ballot.

Critics view Hegseth’s increased emphasis on having troops participate in elections as using his position to influence the forthcoming elections, pointing to the Defense secretary’s campaign appearances in Kentucky and Iowa this year.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

But others argue voting is a direct way for service members to engage in a constitutional system they have pledged to protect and that the military has a responsibility to help service members register and ultimately vote.

Meaghan Mobbs, director of the Center for American Safety and Security at the Independent Women’s Forum, said Hegseth’s election-focused messaging “form is a bit unusual,” but the function is not.

“Yes, a department-wide voting stand-down personally announced by the secretary is more visible than the Pentagon’s normal election messaging,” Mobbs, a former Army paratrooper, told The Hill on Friday. “But the military has a longstanding legal responsibility to help service members register, obtain absentee ballots and vote.”

“As a former soldier, I believe the essential line is nonpartisanship,” Mobbs said. “The military should never tell troops whom to support, but it should ensure that they can participate.”

Typically, service members vote by absentee ballot because they are rarely registered to vote in the state where they are stationed. So having time to go through the candidates and drop off the ballot at the post office can be “valuable,” but it normally does not take a full day, said Carrie A. Lee, a civil-military relations expert and senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund.

“I do worry about whether this stand-down will be interpreted as an order from the secretary directing service members to vote—which would be inappropriate,” Lee told The Hill on Friday.

She noted the Trump administration rescinded executive orders last year allowing all federal workers to take administrative leave to vote and “instead implemented far more restrictive guidance” on whether federal workers could take leave to cast ballots.

“So this stand-down departs significantly from the administration’s policy across the rest of the federal workforce,” Lee said.

During both announcements, Hegseth, a former Army National Guard major, emphasized that Pentagon leadership should not tell service members for whom they should vote but encouraged service members to exercise their right, pointing out that about 300,000 troops did not register to vote two years ago.

The Defense secretary also said the stand-down order will be executed by Oct. 15 and will continue in even-numbered election years.

“Every warrior deserves an opportunity to cast his or her ballot and be confident that it will be counted. Keep our nation the land of the free and the home of the brave,” the Pentagon chief said Friday in a video. “Get registered and vote.”

About 67 percent of active-duty military members were registered to vote in the 2024 election, a 3-point decrease when compared to the 2020 election, according to Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP) data.

Around 71 percent of the 1.3 million active-duty military members are eligible to cast an absentee ballot with special protections because they are stationed away from their voting residence, according to the FVAP.

But involvement has gone down in recent elections. The FVAP estimated the participation rate of active-duty military personnel in 2024 was 42 percent, down from 47 percent in 2020.

Mobbs, a combat veteran of Afghanistan, said Hegseth’s stand-down order is “extremely valuable” because military underparticipation is a “measurable problem.”

“From a national-security perspective, civic participation matters. Our adversaries constantly work to convince Americans that our institutions are corrupt, illegitimate or not worth participating in,” she said. “A military whose members are informed, engaged and invested in our constitutional system is a stronger military.”

In May, Hegseth went to Kentucky to help unseat Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who ran in the GOP primary against former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein, in an unusual move for any Defense secretary.

Pentagon officials said Hegseth was already in Kentucky as part of official duties and attended the event “in his personal capacity .” Some critics pointed to a potential violation of the Hatch Act, which limits the political activities of some federal officials.

Massie ultimately lost the primary. Last month, Massie, a prominent Iran war critic, introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth.

In August, Hegseth campaigned for Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa), who is running for reelection. The Pentagon again explained it was in “a personal capacity.”

Lee, of the German Marshall Fund, said there is “significant precedent” for commanders in chief and administrations to support get-out-the-vote efforts for U.S. service members, though the “biggest” efforts come during wartime when it can be difficult to get absentee ballots to deployed troops.

“For example, during World War II the Roosevelt administration led a big GOTV [get-out-the-vote] effort in 1944 to ensure all deployed GIs were able to vote,” she said. “So it’s unusual that there is such a big emphasis during a midterm election when it’s peacetime, but there is precedent for supporting GOTV during elections.”

Hegseth’s stand-down order will ensure time for service member training, processing and submission of Federal Post Card Applications (FPCA) if they choose to vote by absentee ballot. Commanders have to allow time for troops to coordinate with their Unit Voting Assistance Officers, review state voting requirements and submit the FPCA to ensure “timely receipt of their ballots,” the Defense secretary said in a one-page memo .

Former Trump administration chief strategist Steve Bannon, who has not always backed Hegseth’s Pentagon, praised Hegseth’s stand-down order, saying the Defense secretary “threw down and threw down hard today.”

“I told you it’s Washington, Lincoln and Trump,” Bannon said Friday on his “War Room” show.

Mobbs said time will tell if the order will boost the number of service members who cast votes in the November elections, but Lee argued that anytime access to voting is made “easier,” it will increase turnout.

“I would love to see the administration apply this same philosophy across the entire federal government to ensure everyone has the opportunity to cast their ballot,” she said.

images.caption: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth walks through the basement of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., to a meeting with Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) on June 16, 2026.

articles.title: Asos hackers hijack shopping app’s notifications.
articles.summary:
Users of the Asos app received an unexpected notification from alleged hackers claiming to have “fully compromised” the company’s Snowflake cloud platform, linking to a Telegram channel. The alert may have only gone out to iOS users, since my partner’s Android phone never received it. Asos’ website and app still seem to be working.

articles.title: Latest Trump Account changes: What families need to know now
articles.summary: There is a lot of fine print to know about if your child now has a Trump Account, a new federal savings and investment vehicle.
articles.body:
The Treasury Department announced on October 1 that it had automatically enrolled all eligible children for Trump Accounts, the new federal savings and investment vehicle for kids that went live on July 4.

Until now, parents had to proactively sign up for a Trump Account, but fewer than eight million were opened as of this summer – just a fraction of the tens of millions of children eligible to have one.

"With automatic enrollment, over 60 million more eligible children now have an account ready to be claimed," said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. "This is a transformative milestone in the Trump Administration's effort to give every American child the opportunity to build generational wealth and jump-start their financial future."

The Treasury estimates that the new auto enrollment structure will create an additional two million accounts every year.

"The shift towards automatic enrollment follows best practice from the research and reflects the fact that the previous opt-in structure was producing low participation rates," said Madeline Brown, a senior policy associate at the Urban Institute. "The (new) rulemaking … outlines a first step, which ensures children won't lose out on major philanthropic contributions, or the earnings on those contributions, if no one has opened an account for them."

Even with auto enrollment, however, there is still a lot of fine print to know about if your child now has a Trump Account.

So … we've updated our one-stop-shop FAQ to address your most salient questions from the basics to the nitty gritty.

They are IRA-style investment accounts for eligible children. They are like traditional IRAs in that money in the accounts will grow tax deferred. But the rules for Trump Accounts differ during the so-called "growth period" – which encompasses the first 18 years of a child's life.

The account belongs to the child, but the parent, legal guardian or other authorized adult who will serve as custodian until the child is 18.

Contributions from individuals must be made with after-tax money.

Withdrawals, which generally may not be made until the year the child turns 18,* will be taxed as ordinary income at the child's tax rate – minus the portion attributable to after-tax contributions made over the years, according to the Congressional Research Service.

What are the eligibility rules for kids and adults?

Only children who are US citizens and have a valid Social Security number may have a Trump Account. And no child may have more than one.

images.caption: Who is authorized to open a Trump Account? How much will a child have at age 18? How will the money be taxed? Will it hurt your chance of getting federal benefits? - Chong Kee Siong/E+/Getty Images

articles.title: Exclusive: Glimpse wants to give hardware companies an X-ray view of every critical part | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Called Explore, Glimpse's new image processing software lets hardware makers speed up quality control checks using CT scanners.
articles.body:
Recalls are no joke. Take the one that sidelined every Chevy Bolt made between 2017 and 2022: A problem at an LG battery factory caused some parts inside the cells to be installed improperly, which ultimately cost LG $1.9 billion .

Pretty much every major manufacturer has to deal with recalls. In the EV space alone, Volkswagen, Stellantis, Hyundai, Toyota, and others have all suffered through them.

“The majority of those major quality issues could have been caught with CT scanning. And the reason why they weren’t is because it’s way too slow to do any kind of statistical sampling,” Eric Moch, co-founder and CEO of Glimpse , told TechCrunch.

To help companies find more defects, Glimpse has developed a way for battery manufacturers to inspect cells 10 to 30 times faster by significantly boosting throughput on their existing CT scanners. Using Glimpse’s software, manufacturers could scan tens of thousands of cells per day, up from the current handful, Moch said. A customer “super scanner” that Glimpse is developing with partners could complete a scan in a second or two, he added.

Batteries aren’t the only parts to suffer from costly defects, of course, so Glimpse is launching a new product, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. Called Explore, the product will let customers in industries such as aerospace, automotive, electronics, and medical devices use the startup’s image processing software to speed up quality control checks using CT scanners in their labs and development environments.

Glimpse currently has over 100 customers, such as Anker, Lucid, and the U.S. Navy, and currently generates revenue in the “mid seven-figure” range, Moch said. Customers include both buyers and sellers of batteries.

To wring more speed out of traditionally slow CT scanners, the startup has written its own image processing pipeline, which compresses scans and cleans them up. It’s built around deep learning algorithms, and much of the initial processing happens on edge computers deployed at a customer’s site. “It does all of the heavy lifting before sending the output to the cloud,” Moch said.

Altogether, the combination of quality improvements and compression make for clear images that load within seconds in a web browser, the company claims. “You don’t have to wait minutes or even sometimes hours for that data to load,” he said.

Alongside scanned images, Glimpse’s dashboard will also show customers part measurements they specify. In the case of batteries, it might measure the distance between layers in a battery cell. If they start deviating from the norm, Glimpse’s software will flag it and highlight it in the scanned images. “They can see with their own eyes the defects that they care about,” Moch said. The deep learning algorithms also take into account customer input, retraining themselves along the way.

Customers who don’t have their own CT scanners can ship parts to Glimpse, which will use its own CT scanner in the Boston area. The company said it is opening a second Scan On Demand center in the San Francisco Bay Area.

“We expect this scanning service to actually be a bigger market. You can spend a couple hundred bucks or a few thousand dollars on Glimpse, and you don’t have to buy a very expensive piece of equipment,” Moch said. “And one day, when it makes sense for you, you buy the scanner and then you run our software on top of it.”

articles.title: New York declares measles disaster emergency
articles.summary: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) on Monday declared the first statewide disaster emergency this year over a measles outbreak that has sickened more than 100 people. New York has reported 108 measles cases as of Oct. 3, according to state officials, with most cases occurring outside New York City. Seven cases occurred in the…
articles.body:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) on Monday declared the first statewide disaster emergency this year over a measles outbreak that has sickened more than 100 people.

New York has reported 108 measles cases as of Oct. 3, according to state officials , with most cases occurring outside New York City. Seven cases occurred in the city, while the rest were confirmed elsewhere in the state.

According to state officials, 92 cases have been reported since July 15 in rural communities across 18 counties where vaccination rates are low. Local health departments have administered more than 1,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine in rural areas during that period.

“After reviewing the latest data on measles cases in New York State, I am declaring a State Disaster Emergency to strengthen our ongoing efforts to confront this disease,” Hochul said in a statement. “No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease.”

The declaration, which will remain in effect through Nov. 4, gives health officials broader authority to respond to the outbreak, including expanding the group of medical professionals who can administer measles vaccines and allowing nurses to order testing for suspected cases.

Paramedics, advanced EMS providers, pharmacists and midwives are among those newly authorized to administer vaccines in addition to physicians.

The newly expanded eligible pool allows those individuals to administer the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine to children as young as two-years-old.

The rate of infection also requires providers to report MMR vaccinations to immunization registries within 72 hours.

The emergency declaration comes as neighboring Pennsylvania confronts an even larger outbreak, with cases surpassing 1,000 this week.

The latest Pennsylvania Department of Health dashboard has recorded 1,004 total measles cases in the state so far this year as of Tuesday morning, including 198 hospitalizations and five deaths. A third of those cases occurred in individuals under 18-years-old.

Nearly 3,900 cases have been reported nationwide, the highest annual total since 1991, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention .

articles.title: WHO: No further signs of infections at Russian plague lab
articles.summary: The World Health Organization (WHO) said Monday there were no further signs of infections at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia, following one researcher at the facility reportedly dying from the pneumonic plague. “No case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk, ​Russian Federation,” Russian authorities said in an…
articles.body:
The World Health Organization (WHO) said Monday there were no further signs of infections at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia, following one researcher at the facility reportedly dying from the pneumonic plague .

“No case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk, ​Russian Federation,” Russian authorities said in an official ​response to a WHO request, according to Reuters.

In a separate statement to The Hill’s partner, News Nation, WHO said, “all of the patient’s contacts have reportedly been identified and are being monitored for illness, and none to date have shown symptoms of illness.”

Early testing results “to date are reportedly negative” but it was “unclear for which pathogens” they were tested .

“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low. The risk assessment will be updated once more information is available,” it added.

On Friday, a woman in her late 20s “died of severe pneumonia” in Russia, according to the WHO, citing other reports. The agency stated that no cause of death has been confirmed.

Authorities are investigating whether pneumonic plague caused the researcher’s death, as the research institute in Siberia studied dangerous pathogens, including plague. In the region, plague can also naturally occur in wild animals.

WHO confirmed it had not “received a formal notification about this through [International Health Regulations (IHR)] channels” though the agency believes this may be because Russia is determining whether the event falls under the notifiable categories.

WHO requested information from Russian authorities on the incident on Saturday, which under the IHR, gives Russia 24 hours to respond. It is unclear if Russia has responded to the WHO’s request.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Tuesday he believed its “incumbent” on Russia to share more information on the laboratory where someone died. Rubio did add it’s “irresponsible” to speculate on how the illness will progress .

The Trump administration is monitoring the case in Russia and similarly encouraged Russian authorities to share further information on the incident. It is working closely with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and other interagency partners.

According to the CDC , pneumonic plague “is a rare and often fatal disease that can be transmitted by respiratory droplets from animals or persons infected with Yersinia pestis bacteria.”

articles.title: A Trump Mobile breach may have exposed data of more than 3,600 people
articles.summary: Trump Mobile appears to have suffered a data breach impacting 3,615 customers, according to reports from PCMag and Straight Arrow News.
articles.body: Trump Mobile appears to have suffered a data breach that may have exposed the data of 3,615 people, according to reports from PCMag and Straight Arrow News. The breach reportedly included names, home addresses, emails, phone numbers, and order information. PCMag and Straight Arrow News contacted several individuals in the dataset, who confirmed that the leaked information was accurate. The leaked data may include people who never fully signed up for Trump Mobile, as one person told PCMag that they never managed to set up their account but still gave the company their email address and phone number. It also reportedly includes information related to Eric Brunnett, the chief information technology officer at The Trump Organization. A hacking group called BYOD claimed responsibility for the potential breach. One member told PCMag that they breached the phone service by installing a remote access trojan on an employee of Liberty Mobile — the carrier that powers Trump Mobile’s network. The group also claims to have access to the backend of Trump Mobile’s website, according to Straight Arrow News. The Verge reached out to Trump Mobile with a request for comment but didn’t immediately hear back.

articles.title: Anduril to invest $3.7B in new Baltimore shipyard to build Virginia-class submarine parts
articles.summary: Defense contractor Anduril is planning to invest $3.7 billion into a new shipyard in Sparrows Point, Baltimore, to manufacture parts for Virginia-class submarines. The company secured up to a $2.9 billion contract with the U.S. Navy to help establish the 2 million square-foot facility, dubbed Arsenal-2, that will create more than 3,000 jobs in Maryland. …
articles.body:
Defense contractor Anduril is planning to invest $3.7 billion into a new shipyard in Sparrows Point, Baltimore, to manufacture parts for Virginia-class submarines.

The company secured up to a $2.9 billion contract with the U.S. Navy to help establish the 2 million square-foot facility, dubbed Arsenal-2, that will create more than 3,000 jobs in Maryland.

“This is about putting more food on the table and being able to meet requirements that our country has to produce more submarines,” Chris Brose, Anduril’s president and chief strategy officer, said during a press briefing.

Brose said the goal is to produce more torpedo tubes.

The Virginia-class submarines, nuclear-powered attack submarines which have vertical launching system-launched cruise missile capability, are jointly built by HII’s Newport News Shipbuilding and General Dynamics Electric Boat.

“This massive new project will deliver the largest private investment and create the most jobs in Maryland in over a decade — driving billions of dollars in economic activity that will boost Maryland families not just in Baltimore County, but throughout the state,” said Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) said in a statement .

“With this facility, thousands of Marylanders will have new pathways to work, wages, and wealth through advanced training and high-skilled maritime manufacturing jobs,” Moore added.

The new Baltimore facility comes as the Virginia-class submarine has faced setbacks with a shortage of experienced workers and late delivery of materials, according to a July report from the Government Accountability Office (GAO).

“As we’ve dug into this work and really worked closely with administration and with the Navy, we’ve really seen the problems that exist in this program are problems that we can uniquely contribute to,” Brose said.

The company’s co-founder Palmer Luckey was also recently tapped as one of three people — alongside SpaceX AI CEO Elon Musk and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.) — to lead the Pentagon’s new group to study the future of warfare called “ Project Meridian .”

A senior administration official told reporters on Tuesday that $2.9 billion for the facility will come from the Pentagon and the Trump administration expects the funding to fit into the regular budget process.

articles.title: Red-dyed diesel: What is it, and can you use the tax-free fuel?
articles.summary: President Trump on Monday signed an order to extend the use of red-dyed diesel, but what is it?
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Diesel prices have been high as of late, prompting President Trump to announce new efforts to lower costs on Monday.

As expected, those efforts included expanding access to red-dyed diesel. It should, in theory, be more affordable, but it isn’t quite that simple. It may also not have the largest impact, experts warn.

Here’s what to know about the diesel, including whether or not your vehicle can use it.

Simply put, it’s diesel with red dye added.

The dye is meant to indicate that the fuel is exempt from state excise taxes and the 24.4-cents-per-gallon federal tax. The coloring also helps “law enforcement … identify it to enforce penalties and back taxes for on-road use,” a fact sheet from the White House explains.

Sure, if you operate a vehicle that runs on diesel.

Red-dyed fuel is already available to farmers, for example, who use it for off-road use, explains Patrick De Haan of GasBuddy, a platform that monitors national gasoline and diesel prices.

Other uses, like in construction equipment, marine vessels and generators, may require a license , according to the Washington State Department of Licensing.

The newest push by Trump is meant to expand the fuel to truck drivers and those operating diesel vehicles. However, De Haan noted that “most major truck stops don’t sell dyed diesel.”

It’s unclear whether red-dyed diesel would expand to more fueling stations.

C NRG Fleet, a commercial fuel card company, does offer a map of stations that sell dyed diesel. It includes stations in nearly every state. Lacking locations are Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, Alaska, and Hawaii.

Another map of off-road diesel locations from the Commercial Fueling Network does, however, include locations in Rhode Island and Connecticut.

In essence, yes. If you no longer have to pay a tax on the fuel, the price should go down.

Trump said Monday that a “typical trucker will save more than $100 every time they fill up.”

His order, more specifically, calls for a deferral of payment “of the Federal excise tax imposed for on-road use of dyed diesel fuel for the remainder of the year without interest or penalties, and to explore pathways to eliminate the obligation to pay the deferred taxes.”

Tom Kloza, chief oil analyst at Gulf Oil, previously told The Hill that he doesn’t expect that increasing availability of red-dyed diesel will make a significant difference in the price overall. Instead, he called it “really a cosmetic gesture.”

“This really is a Band-Aid where a tourniquet would be more appropriate.”

De Haan shared similar remarks on X on Monday.

“States have their own dyed diesel laws, and an [executive] order can’t override them,” he explained in a thread . North Dakota , for example, has a tax of 4 cents per gallon on dyed diesel.

Late last month, Texas expanded the use of dyed diesel for on-road use for truckers and farmers, Nexstar’s KXAN reported. Indiana made a similar move last week, suspending restrictions for agriculture and timber harvesting operations on its roads, according to Nexstar’s WEHT. Other states to take action regarding dyed diesel lately include Oklahoma , North Dakota , North Carolina , Nebraska , Missouri , Louisiana , Arkansas , and Alabama .

De Haan further noted that guidance from the White House suggested the tax is “‘deferred,’ not eliminated.”

He also said last week that supply is the problem, not taxes, when it comes to diesel.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

images.caption: The price of a gallon of diesel fuel is shown electronically on a pump at a QuikTrip station Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Greenwood Village, Colo. (AP Photo/David Zalubowski)

articles.title: We can’t just change the definition of ‘recording’
articles.summary: AI hardware companies are pushing forward a new definition for recording devices. But should they be allowed to without societal consensus?
articles.body: With AI hardware, tech companies are pushing the definition of what does and doesn’t constitute a recording. For most of gadget history, it’d be reasonable to assume that a device with a microphone or camera is either recording you or it isn’t; it’s either on or off, without much gray area. Microphones capture sound. Cameras capture images. That data is saved onto a device. Sometimes, it’s also sent to the cloud — hopefully with end-to-end encryption — for processing. That data is a preserved instant in time and is therefore a recording. Perhaps not anymore. Last week, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that Apple is working on a smart home camera that doesn’t save video recordings. Instead, AI uses the visual data to create text snippets that describe what’s happening around your home. Supposedly, it’ll support facial recognition, but without video footage. The idea is that it still protects some privacy. This tech, Gurman says, is similar to how the cameras in rumored future AirPods will also work. It’s similar to Apple’s Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. The Apple Watch has had a microphone for ages, mostly for Siri and taking phone calls from the wrist. Of the four Audio Intelligence features, two have caused the most debate online: Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former produces a transcript of the past 15 seconds, whereas the latter can generate high-level summaries of the conversations you have throughout the day. [Image: All Audio Intelligence features are opt-in. As you can see in this photo, Apple states in its Music Detection language that it “does not record audio.” But once a song is detected, is that not a record that you heard that song? In other words, Ray-Ban Meta glasses take photos and record video, which is stored on your phone. This rumored Apple approach would mean cameras can see you, microphones can hear you — but neither is “saving” anything. Does this count as recording? Apple doesn’t comment on rumors, but based on how it’s publicly communicated its Audio Intelligence privacy philosophy, I’d argue the company doesn’t think so. Apple says these features don’t save any audio. The raw data is deleted once it’s finished processing in a separate, secure exclave on the S11 processor. Any information sent to the cloud is through private cloud compute and is therefore inaccessible to Apple or third parties. It’s not just Apple, either. Sandeep Waraich, Google’s senior director of wearables, told The Verge in a conversation that Google is also mulling this concept. What if, he posited, cameras on smart glasses didn’t record data? For example, if the glasses could process visual data in your environment using AI, but didn’t save any footage for posterity. In that way, Waraich argued, the camera could “just” be an image sensor. By these definitions, something has to be preserved and reviewable to be “recording” you. But wouldn’t any text transcripts generated by a smart home camera or smartwatch count as preserved and reviewable? Or, in trying to make AI hardware more palatable, are tech companies relying on what can be subpoenaed in court? It might seem silly to argue semantics, but multiple concepts are being tested here. Whatever your personal opinions about privacy, it’s generally agreed that you can do whatever you want with your own data. Before gadgets could “always listen,” they slotted into public and private spaces more seamlessly. This new crop of gadgets, however, asks you to be a more active steward of other people’s privacy. After all, humans don’t live in hermetically sealed bubbles. We live, work, and hang out in a multitude of environments — some private, others public, and plenty in a gray area. The rules for a restaurant differ from those of a theater, office, or sporting venue. They’re vastly different from a public restroom, even though these are all at least semi-public spaces. Even if you “record” everything you see in your mind, human memories can’t be shared objectively. They’re colored by biases and warped by perspective. Recordings are less subjective and arguably factual. There’s also the question of signaling intent in the absence of universally understood norms. Take Meta’s smart glasses. They use a white, pulsing “privacy light” to indicate when someone’s recording video. Conversely, the universal color for recording lights is red, so a less tech-savvy person may not even know what a white light signifies. (These are, after all, still niche products.) Even without modification, white privacy lights are easily obscured by bangs and a bright sunny day. This is also a new norm; other smart glasses or AI hardware companies aren’t obligated to signal this intent in the same way as Meta. An AI ring or pendant that records audio or video may have no light at all. [Image: Would you notice this privacy light in person? Even more confusing, products that can record increasingly look like products that can’t. That could be exacerbated even further if tech companies begin adding cameras that don’t record visual footage. If we start adding cameras to smart glasses that don’t record video footage, how will you tell them apart from pairs that do? If an Oura Ring — which has no microphone — looks like a Vocci Ring — which does — and both look like regular rings, what is the average person supposed to do? Right now, hardware seems to be the main focus of the surveillance tech debate. There’s a sense that getting rid of cameras solves the problem. It doesn’t, though it makes it harder to use this tech in nefarious ways. But arguably, it’s not the camera or microphone that gives people the ick. The queasy feeling comes from knowing a preserved snippet of you can exist in someone else’s device with no knowledge of how it’ll be used. This is where all the tension surrounding AI hardware converges. For AI to be “good” and truly personal in the way Big Tech imagines, it has to know a lot about you — and the people in your life. It has to “see” what you see, hear what you hear, and learn from your day-to-day actions. To do that, it has to “remember” these things. So in some ways, it must record your life and everything that happens in it. The incentives for Big Tech to collect this data are obvious: Personal data is money, money is power, and power is influence. What’s less clear is what society gets from this tradeoff. Vague promises of helpfulness and convenience? [Image: This Vocci Ring can record conversations and its privacy light is extremely hard to notice. Regardless, it’s clear tech companies have decided to barrel forward with stuffing AI into every existing gadget while inventing new form factors. Right now, it’s most clear in phones and wearables, but these considerations are soon headed to the smart home, TVs, laptops, tablets, and headphones. Likely in ways consumers have yet to consider. What we allow these AI gadgets to remember will rewrite culture as we know it. This is why we must reach a societal consensus on what constitutes a recording — and who, if anyone, gets to change that definition.

articles.title: The FCC has decertified two more Chinese test labs.
articles.summary:
The US has been finding ways to stem the tide of imported Chinese gadgets, including decertifying “bad labs” that are “apparently controlled by China.” It’s now pulled credentials from two more: SLG-CPC Test Laboratory, and Shenzhen STS Test Services, “for willfully providing incorrect or false equipment test results in connection with applications for equipment authorization.”
It’s also planning to do the same to Shenzhen CTB Testing.

articles.title: Democratic senator says Pentagon denied him access to US base in Qatar ‘to hide the costs’ of Iran war
articles.summary: Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), says the Pentagon blocked him from a key U.S. military base in Qatar while he traveling in the Middle East, accusing the Trump administration of trying to hide damage caused by the Iran war. Murphy, who traveled to Doha, Qatar, and later Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, as part of a congressional delegation,…
articles.body:
Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), says the Pentagon blocked him from a key U.S. military base in Qatar while he traveling in the Middle East, accusing the Trump administration of trying to hide damage caused by the Iran war.

Murphy, who traveled to Doha, Qatar, and later Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, as part of a congressional delegation, said he attempted to visit the Al Udeid Air Base — the largest U.S. base in the region that Iran has repeatedly attacked since the war began in late February.

Prior to the trip, Murphy said he wanted “to see firsthand the impact of the Iran War, the damage it’s caused to our facilities in the region, and how it’s harmed our relationships with partners in the region.”

But after being barred from visiting Al Udeid, Murphy said, “There is an active, unprecedented, unconstitutional effort underway to hide the costs of this war and the implications of this war from Congress and the American people,” as reported by Reuters .

He also said that the Defense Department refused to set up a briefing for him on the war while he was in the region.

“I’ve never encountered anything like this in my time in the Senate and it’s part of a deliberate campaign of obfuscation that my Republican colleagues in Congress should demand an end to,” Murphy added.

Asked about Murphy’s accusations, a senior Pentagon official told The Hill that the senator’s office was informed prior to his trip to the Middle East that he would not receive Defense Department support to access Al Udeid, pointing to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s March directive on travel restrictions in the region.

“That decision was communicated in advance by the Office of the Secretary of War for Legislative Affairs. The Department applies the Secretary’s guidance evenly,” the official said in a statement.

Murphy, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and the first Democratic lawmaker to visit the region since the start of the Iran war, made clear that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had helped make the trip possible and arranged meetings with senior Gulf officials.

But the Connecticut senator has called out President Trump for having no clear plan to end the conflict, which now has a price tag of more than $45 billion.

The Pentagon also continues to face scrutiny over its opacity about the mounting toll from the conflict, which has dragged on for more than seven months.

The U.S. military has placed the number of service members who have died in the Middle East since the start of the conflict at 19. Last month, however, The Washington Post reported that there are at least 23 military fatalities.

“[Defense Secretary] Pete Hegseth has been hiding the cost of the war, the extent of its damages, and the loss of American life from the public and from Congress,” Murphy said prior to the trip.

articles.title: Hegseth to welcome USS Abraham Lincoln in San Diego after lengthy deployment
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will travel to San Diego on Tuesday and will welcome the USS Abraham Lincoln crew home on Wednesday after the aircraft carrier extended its deployment to the Middle East. According to the Pentagon, Hegseth will speak with the ship’s crew, participate in physical training and eat lunch with the service members…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will travel to San Diego on Tuesday and will welcome the USS Abraham Lincoln crew home on Wednesday after the aircraft carrier extended its deployment to the Middle East.

According to the Pentagon, Hegseth will speak with the ship’s crew, participate in physical training and eat lunch with the service members while in San Diego.

The USS Abraham Lincoln, a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, is coming back to the U.S. after an extended deployment in the Middle East, which prompted pushback from congressional Democrats and some former defense officials over reports of degrading mental health of crew on board, tight food supply and poor living conditions.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Top administration officials, including the defense secretary, defended the conditions onboard the aircraft carrier, which spent more than 280 days without a port call.

“Listen, we make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment,” Hegseth said in August . “Some deployments are longer than others, and I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody. What they do in those high seas and those austere conditions with less port calls, it’s incredible.”

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee, last month that eight sailors assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during a grueling deployment, which included military operations against Iran.

A carrier strike group is normally made up of an aircraft carrier, cruisers, destroyers or frigates and a host of aircraft.

Rep. Sara Jacobs (D-Ca.), who is on the House Armed Services Committee, visited the aircraft carrier late last month as part of a bipartisan delegation to conduct in-person oversight of the conditions onboard.

“Oversight can’t wait until the USS Abraham Lincoln comes home to San Diego. We deserve answers and accountability now,” Rep. Sara Jacobs (D-Ca.), who sits on the House Armed Services Committee, said in a statement on Sept. 27 after a bipartisan delegation conducted in-person oversight of the conditions onboard.

She added, “That’s why I traveled aboard the ship today to conduct oversight in-person. I raised my concerns directly with the ship’s command and received a briefing on logistics, supply issues and lessons learned for future deployments.”

articles.title: Medicare for All support soars to 66 percent in 6 years: KFF poll
articles.summary: Support for Medicare for All jumped to 66 percent among U.S. adults in 2026, highest since 2016, according to polling results published Tuesday. Health research group KFF found that 32 percent of those surveyed strongly favored “having a national health plan … in which all Americans would get their insurance from a single government plan,”…
articles.body:
Support for Medicare for All jumped to 66 percent among U.S. adults in 2026, highest since 2016, according to polling results published Tuesday.

Health research group KFF found that 32 percent of those surveyed strongly favored “having a national health plan … in which all Americans would get their insurance from a single government plan,” a stance commonly referred to as Medicare for All. It also found support for the policy was up by around 13-points from when the question was last posed in 2020.

An additional 34 percent somewhat supported the plan, while 15 percent somewhat opposed it and 19 percent strongly opposed.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

KKF noted that respondents’ evaluation of the single-payer system was divided on party lines, with 84 percent of Democrats favoring the policy and 66 percent of Republicans opposing it. Among independents, Medicare for All’s approval reached 72 percent.

The group also found Americans’ opinions on national health plans sway based upon “any public debate in which the public hears arguments for and against such a plan.” For example, the percentage of respondents who opposed Medicare for All reached 76 percent when they heard it could cause potential delays in medical appointments or treatments.

Sixty-four percent opposed the plan if it caused tax hikes, while 61 percent said they would be against a national health program if it threatened the current Medicare system.

On the other hand, Medicare for All reached 76 percent when those polled heard that the policy may guarantee health insurance as a right for all Americans, and 52 percent backed such a program if it eliminates health insurance premiums.

The latter results mark a departure from October 2020, when the prospect of Medicare for All eliminating private insurance companies led to lower support for the plan — at 37 percent. Fifty-eight percent opposed the measure in the case that it made private health insurance obsolete.

Each of these claims shifted respondents’ opinions across the board, regardless of partisanship and age.

A group of progressive lawmakers attempted to solve rising healthcare concerns through the Medicare for All Act , introduced by Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) in April 2025. It was co-sponsored by 117 House Democrats but was opposed by GOP lawmakers, who argued it was too radical.

However, as a national health plan gained support, health care affordability concerns remain a top issue among voters — who trust Democrats over Republicans on the issue by a nearly two-to-one margin, according to KKF.

About half of voters said it is “extremely important” for candidates in the midterm elections to talk about the cost of health care, the survey found.

The poll was conducted among 1,328 respondents between Sept. 16 – 21. Its margin of error is plus or minus 3 percentage points.
